chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali from his father from Hammad ibn Isa and Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'When the Muhrim (one in Ihram) catches the game in the Haram (sanctuary) while he is Muhrim, it is appropriate for him to bury it and no one should eat it. And if he catches it in the Hill (non-sanctuary), then the Halal (one not in Ihram) eats it and the fidyah (ransom/compensation) is upon him.' The meaning in it is also what we mentioned: that if he catches it while it is alive, it is permissible for the Muhill (one who ends Ihram) to slaughter it and eat it. And it is also permissible that the intended meaning is if he killed it by throwing at it and did not slaughter it, then if the matter is thus, it is permissible for the Muhill to eat it, not the Muhrim. And the first narrations encompassed the one who slaughtered while he was Muhrim, and the slaughtering is not from the throwing in anything. And that which confirms what we mentioned from that what the Muhrim slaughtered is not permissible to eat in any state is what he narrated:

key_terms.الْمُحِلُّ: One who has ended the state of Ihram
key_terms.الْمُحْرِمُ: One in the state of Ihram (pilgrimal consecration)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating game caught by a pilgrim in Ihram in the Haram versus the Hill?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi elaborates on the distinction between killing by throwing (ramy) versus direct slaughter, noting that while the primary narration addresses direct slaughter, the ruling extends to game caught alive where the Muhrim does not eat it. This clarification ensures that the prohibition of consuming the game remains strict for the pilgrim regardless of the method, reinforcing the sanctity of the Ihram state. The text underscores the importance of fidyah as a compensatory measure for violating the spatial restrictions of the Haram.
